replies.What is your relationship with mathemati: I’ve never had formal math education, so I don’t understand equations or formulas. I enjoy reading about chemistry and literature, which are more accessible to me. I see math as something distant, like a language I didn’t learn. I don’t use it daily, but I respect how it helps solve real-world problems.
replies.Do you ever get anxious when thinking ab: Yes, I get anxious when I hear about math. It feels like a foreign language I can’t speak. My mind races, and I worry I’ll make a mistake. I don’t have a background in it, so every equation seems like a puzzle I can’t solve. I try to calm myself by focusing on what I know, like stories or games.
replies.Did you ever use AI to support your math: No, I haven’t used AI for math learning. I don’t have the confidence or time to explore it. I’ve tried reading about math in novels or games, but it never felt like a real lesson. I’d prefer learning through stories or football, where numbers are part of the fun, not the focus.
replies.How would you explain, step by step, how: I don’t know how to solve second-order equations. I’ve never studied algebra beyond basic arithmetic. I can’t follow steps like factoring or using the quadratic formula. I’d need someone to teach me slowly, like a story, with examples I can relate to, like football scores or game rules.

I don’t understand what stationary points are. I’ve never studied calculus or functions. I can’t follow steps like taking derivatives or setting them to zero. I’d need a simple story to explain it—like how a ball rolls to a stop on a hill—before I could even begin to grasp it.
replies.Briefly, how do you perform a Principal: Principal Component Analysis? I’ve never heard of it. It sounds like a complex math tool. I don’t have the background to perform it. I’d get anxious because it seems like a maze of numbers. But I can imagine it as a way to sort things—like organizing books by theme—without needing to do the math myself.
replies.According to you, how can LLMs be used t: LLMs could help by turning math into stories—like how a football team uses strategy or how a novel has a plot with patterns. Instead of equations, students could learn through games or tales. This would make math less scary and more relatable. It’s not about solving problems, but understanding patterns in life.
